paragraphs.text: ON THE GREAT MARTYR THEODORE. You, the people of Christ, the holy flock, the royal priesthood, you crowds who have streamed together from every side, from the cities and from the countryside: where did you get the signal for the journey that has led you to this holy place? Who laid on you so urgent a need to be here, and to be here on time? And this in the winter season, when war is at rest, the soldier puts away his armor, the sailor hangs his rudder above the smoke, and the farmer takes his ease, tending his plough-oxen at the manger! Is it not plain that the holy martyr sounded the trumpet from the army rolls, stirred many people from different homelands, and called them to his own resting place and

hearth? He did not do it to equip them for war. He did it to gather them to a sweet peace, the peace that best befits Christians. For it was he, we believe, who last year calmed the barbarian storm and halted the terrible war of the savage Scythians. When they were already in sight and close at hand, he brandished at them a fearful weapon. It was not a triple-crested helmet, nor a well-sharpened sword flashing in the sun, but the all-powerful cross of Christ that wards off evil. He himself suffered for that cross, and so won this glory. Now, you servants of this pure religion and lovers of the martyrs, turn your minds to this and consider with me how great a thing a righteous man is, and what rewards he is found worthy of. I mean the rewards in this world and among us, for no one is able to reckon the magnificence of the unseen ones. And when you have marked out the fruit of piety, emulate the resolve of those who are so honored. Desire the prizes that Christ awards to his athletes as they deserve. In the meantime, if you agree, since the enjoyment of the good things to come is still deferred (good hope keeps it in store for the righteous until the Judge of our lives comes), let us look at the present state of the saints and see how very fine and magnificent it is. The soul has gone up and dwells gladly in its own allotted portion, living without a body among its like. The body was the soul's venerable and spotless instrument, and it never harmed the incorruptibility of its indweller by passions of its own. It has been laid out with great honor and care, and it lies reverently in a holy place, like some precious treasure kept for the time of the rebirth. There is no comparing it with the other bodies that have been dissolved by the common death that befalls anyone, even though they are of the same material by nature. Other remains are loathsome to most people. No one passes a tomb with pleasure. If someone happens on an open one and casts his eye on the shapeless things lying inside, he is filled with utter disgust, groans heavily over the human lot, and hurries past. But when someone comes to a place like this one, where our assembly meets today, where there is the memorial of a righteous man and a holy relic, he is first delighted by the magnificence of what he sees. He beholds a house finished like a temple of God, splendid in the size of its building and the beauty of its decoration. Here the carpenter has shaped wood into the likeness of animals, and the stonemason has polished the slabs to the smoothness of silver. The painter too has spread out the flowers of his art. He has pictured the martyr's feats of valor, his resistance, his torments, the bestial faces of the tyrants, their abuses, that flame-fed furnace, the most blessed end of the athlete, and the image in human form of Christ, who presides over the contest. He has worked all this for us in colors, as in a book that speaks, and so he has told the martyr's struggles clearly and made the church as bright as a meadow. For painting knows how to speak even in silence on a wall, and how to do the greatest good.

The mosaicist too has made the floor we walk on worthy of a history. When the visitor has delighted his eyes with these works of art for the senses, he then longs to approach the coffin itself, believing that to touch it is sanctification and blessing. If someone lets him carry away the dust lying on the surface of the resting place, he receives the dust as a gift and stores up the earth as a treasure. And if some stroke of good fortune ever gives him the chance to touch the relic itself, those who have had that experience and have satisfied that longing know how much it is desired, and that it is the gift of the highest prayer. Those who see it embrace it as if it were the living, flourishing body itself, bringing it to their eyes, mouth and ears, to all their senses. Then, shedding tears of reverence and of deep feeling, they make their plea for intercession to the martyr as if he were present whole and in view. They implore him as a bodyguard of God and call on him as one who receives gifts whenever he wishes. From all this, O pious people, learn that "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones." The body of every human being is one and the same, made from one lump of clay. But a body that has simply died is tossed aside like any ordinary thing, while a body graced by the suffering of martyrdom is so beloved and so contended for, as the account above has shown. Therefore let us trust in what is unseen because of what is seen, and in the promise of things to come because of our experience in this world. For many people put their belly, their vainglory and the rubbish of this life before everything else. They think the future is nothing and suppose that everything is over at the end of life. But you who think so, learn the great things from the small ones, and perceive the originals from their shadows. Which of the kings is honored with such honor? Which of the most eminent men who have ever lived is glorified with such remembrance? Which of the generals who took walled cities and enslaved countless nations is as celebrated in song as this soldier? He was a poor man and a new recruit. Paul armed him, angels anointed him for the contest, and Christ crowned him when he had won. But since my speech has come close to the martyr's contests, come, let us leave general matters aside and speak about the saint in particular, for each of us loves what is his own. The noble man's homeland, then, was the land toward the rising sun. Like Job, he too was well-born among the people of the east, and since he shared Job's homeland he did not fall short in imitating his character. But now he is a martyr common to the whole world, a citizen of everything under the sun. He was taken from there to the military rolls…

[?] …that, given time to reflect, he might change his mind for the better." For those madmen called self-control madness, and piety a frenzy and derangement, just as drunkards reproach the sober with their own condition. But the pious man, the soldier of Christ, used the respite he was given for a manly deed. What deed? Now is the time for you to welcome the story with gladness. In the metropolis of Amasea there was a temple to the so-called mother of the gods. The people who were then in error had built it in their folly somewhere there along the banks of the river. Using the time of the reprieve he had been granted, the noble man watched for a suitable hour and a favorable wind, set the temple on fire and burned it down. So by his deed he gave the wicked the answer they were surely expecting from him after his reflection. The deed quickly became known to everyone, since the fire blazed up in full view in the middle of the city. He did not hide what he had done or try to avoid notice. He showed himself openly, exulting greatly in his achievement and rejoicing exceedingly at the turmoil of the godless, who were in an uproar of grief over their temple and wooden idol. He was then denounced to the magistrates as the man who had set the fire with his own hands. So there was a second trial, more fearsome than the first, as was only natural now that so great a provocation had been added. The magistrates took their places on the judgment seat. Theodore spoke freely in their midst. Though he stood as the accused, he had the confidence of a ruler, and when he was questioned, he cut the question short with the speed of his confession. Since he was undaunted and paid no heed to the horrors they threatened, they switched to the opposite approach. They spoke to the righteous man kindly and tried to lure him away with promises. "Know this," they said. "If you are willing to accept our advice and obey it, we will at once make you renowned instead of obscure, honored instead of inglorious. We even promise you the rank of high priest." When he heard about the rank of high priest, the thrice-blessed man laughed long and said: "I judge even the priests of the idols to be wretched, and I pity them as servants of a futile practice. The high priests I pity and loathe all the more. Among the bad, the greater and higher in rank is the more wretched, just as among the unjust it is the more unjust, among murderers the more savage, and among the licentious the more wanton. So you are already casting me down with your ruinous promises. Without realizing it, sirs, you have promised me the very summit of evils. But for anyone who chooses to live piously and rightly, it is better to be cast aside in the house of God than to dwell in the tents of sinners. I pity even these emperors whose lawless law you keep reading aloud. The power of empire is dignity enough among men, yet they have taken on themselves the title of high priest as well. Because of it they wrap themselves in that mournful, dark purple in imitation of the wretched high priests, wearing a gloomy garment with a glorious office. And sometimes, when they approach a foul altar, instead of emperors they become

cooks. They sacrifice birds, rummage through the entrails of wretched cattle, and stain their clothes with gore like butchers." After the righteous man said these things, the magistrates no longer showed even their feigned, put-on kindness. They called him most impious toward the gods, and an insulter and blasphemer of the emperors too. First they hung him on the wooden rack and tore at his body. The executioners worked hard, but he was steadfast and unyielding, and he sang a verse of the Psalms over his tortures: "I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall be in my mouth continually." They scraped away his flesh, and he sang psalms as if someone else were undergoing the punishment. Prison came after this punishment, and there too a wonder happened around the saint. At night the voices of a crowd singing psalms were heard, and those outside saw a light like the lamps that shine at an all-night vigil. The jailer was alarmed at the strange sight and sound and rushed into the cell, but he found no one except the martyr, who was at rest, and the other prisoners, who were asleep. Many such things happened, and he only grew stronger in his confession and his piety. At last the sentence of condemnation came against him, and he was ordered to be perfected by fire. He himself set out on the fair and blessed journey to God, but he left us the memory of his contest as a lesson. He gathers peoples, teaches the church, drives out demons, and brings down angels of peace. He asks God for what is good for us. He has made this place a clinic for all kinds of diseases, a harbor for those tossed by the storms of affliction, a well-stocked storehouse for the poor, a welcoming inn for travelers, and an unceasing festival for those who keep feast. We celebrate this day with a yearly feast, but the crowd of those hurrying here never stops, and the highway leading here looks like a trail of ants, with some going up and others making way for those who are coming. So, O blessed one, by the kindness of the Creator we have reached the turn of the year and gathered your festival for you, this holy assembly of those who love the martyrs. We worship our common Master and keep the victory celebration of your contests. Now come to us, wherever you may be, as overseer of the feast. You called us, and so we call you in return. Perhaps you live high up in the ether, or travel around some heavenly vault, or, ranked among the choirs of

angels, stand beside the Master, or worship him as a faithful servant together with the powers and authorities. Wherever you are, excuse yourself from things there for a little while and come to those who honor you, an unseen friend. See what is being done, so that you may give God double thanks, since for one suffering and one pious confession he has granted you such rewards. May you take joy in your blood and in the pain of the fire. As many crowds as watched your punishment then, so many now serve your honor. We need many benefits. Intercede for your homeland with the common King. A martyr's homeland is the land where he suffered, and his fellow citizens and kinsmen are those who laid him out, keep him and honor him. We fear afflictions and we expect dangers. The accursed Scythians are not far off [?], in labor with war against us. Fight for us as a soldier. As a martyr, use your freedom of speech on behalf of your fellow servants. You have passed beyond this life, but you know the sufferings and needs of humankind. Ask for peace, so that these festivals may not cease, so that no raging, lawless barbarian may run riot against churches or altars, and so that no profane man may trample on holy things. We credit to you the kindness of our having been kept from harm, and we ask for safety in the future too. If more pleading is needed, gather the choir of your brothers the martyrs and pray together with them all. Let the prayers of many righteous men loose the sins of peoples and nations. Remind Peter, rouse Paul, and John as well, the theologian and beloved disciple, so that they may care for the churches they founded, for which they wore chains and bore dangers and deaths. Pray that idolatry may not raise its head against us, that heresies may not sprout like thorns in the vineyard, and that tares may not spring up and choke the wheat. Pray that no rock may rise against us that lacks the richness of the true dew and leaves the power of the word without root and without fruit. Instead, O you who are wondrous among the martyrs, by the power of your intercession and of those with you, may the commonwealth of Christians prove a shining crop that lasts to the end in the rich and fruitful field of faith in Christ, ever bearing the fruit of eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. With him, to the Father together with the Holy Spirit, be glory, power and honor, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
